name: Bouvet Island

pin.note: Approximate centre of the island, from the 54°25′S, 3°20′E coordinates given by the Norwegian Polar Institute

territory: Norway (Norwegian dependency, not part of the Kingdom proper; island and territorial waters are a nature reserve since 1971)

creatures.status_note: Chosen as the best-verified threatened species with a documented Bouvet breeding population. A mammal was not chosen: the Antarctic fur seal and southern elephant seal occur on Bouvet, but a threatened status was not verified in the fetched sources. The IUCN site could not be fetched; status comes from BirdLife South Africa and Wikipedia.

facts.statement: The island lies at roughly 54°25′S, 3°20′E in the South Atlantic Ocean.
facts.evidence_note: Coordinates listed in the location section of the page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Bouvet Island covers about 49 km² and measures roughly 9.5 km by 7 km.
facts.evidence_note: Size figures in the geography summary.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Norwegian Polar Institute puts Gough Island, about 1,600 km away, as the island's nearest land, and the national encyclopedia agrees.
facts.evidence_note: Distances given in the location section; SNL gives the same Gough figure.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: NASA's Earth Observatory describes Bouvet as the world's most remote island, with Antarctica, the nearest land, more than 1,600 km to the south.
facts.evidence_note: Remoteness statement in the image caption text.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The average sea-level temperature on Bouvetøya is about -1 °C, in a maritime Antarctic climate.
facts.evidence_note: Climate paragraph of the page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Monthly mean temperatures run from about 1 °C in January to about -3 °C in September.
facts.evidence_note: Monthly averages cited in the climate paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island is usually wrapped in fog, so helicopter landings often involve waiting, and ocean swell makes boat landings hazardous.
facts.source_title: Bouvetøya: nature reserve rules and visitor advice
facts.evidence_note: Weather notes in the visitor advice section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia gives a February mean near 2 °C, an August mean near -4 °C, and a record low of -18.7 °C.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia's text reports a peak temperature of 14 °C in March 1980, while its own climate table lists 10.6 °C as the highest value.
facts.evidence_note: Internal inconsistency noted between the climate text and table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The highest point is Olavtoppen, 780 m above sea level.
facts.evidence_note: Highest peak given in the area and ice section; SNL and Wikipedia agree.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Britannica gives the island's maximum elevation as 935 m (3,068 ft) and its area as about 59 km², figures that differ from the Norwegian sources (780 m, 49 km²).
facts.evidence_note: Quick-facts style summary at the top of the entry.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Norwegian sources state that about 89% of the island is covered by glaciers or ice.
facts.evidence_note: Ice cover figure in the area section; SNL gives the same percentage.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia states that 93% of the island is glaciated, differing from the Norwegian 89% figure.
facts.evidence_note: Ice cover figure in the geography section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island is the exposed top of a basaltic volcano rising from the deep ocean floor, and it is the southernmost island on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
facts.evidence_note: Geology paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia reports the last eruption was around 2000 BCE, producing a lava flow at Cape Meteor.
facts.evidence_note: Geology section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The national encyclopedia says volcanic activity continues above and below water, though the central crater has probably not erupted for several hundred thousand years; this differs from the eruption date in Wikipedia.
facts.evidence_note: Geology paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Frenchman Jean-Baptiste Charles Bouvet de Lozier sighted the island on 1 January 1739 but did not land.
facts.evidence_note: Discovery section; SNL and Britannica also give 1739.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Norwegian sources say the first landing was in 1822, while Wikipedia credits a British landing by Norris in 1825 and calls an earlier American landing claim disputed.
facts.evidence_note: Discovery paragraph; compared with Wikipedia's discovery section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A Norwegian expedition led by Harald Horntvedt claimed the island on 1 December 1927, and a royal resolution of 23 January 1928 placed it under Norwegian sovereignty.
facts.evidence_note: Annexation paragraph; Wikipedia gives the same dates.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 1930 law made Bouvetøya a Norwegian dependency, and the annexation was motivated by whaling interests.
facts.evidence_note: Annexation paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A CCAMLR ecosystem-monitoring site was established at Nyrøysa on an expedition running from 9 December 1996 to 22 February 1997.
facts.evidence_note: Opening description of the monitoring programme.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Norvegia field station was set up in January 2014, and Norwegian Polar Institute monitoring has run since 1976; Wikipedia instead dates a new station to December 2012.
facts.evidence_note: Station sentence; conflicts with Wikipedia's date.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Bouvet Island is uninhabited; Britannica notes the Norwegian government declared it a nature reserve in 1971.
facts.evidence_note: Status line of the entry.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island and its territorial waters were designated a nature reserve on 17 December 1971.
facts.source_title: Regulations for the protection of Bouvet Island with adjacent territorial waters as a nature reserve (BB-NO-55)
facts.evidence_note: Catalogue record gives the creation date of the regulations.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Reserve rules protect animals, nests and eggs year-round and bar dogs ashore; helicopter landings need a special Norwegian Polar Institute permit.
facts.source_title: Bouvetøya: nature reserve rules and visitor advice
facts.evidence_note: Nature reserve rules section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Vegetation is limited to mosses, lichens, fungi and algae; Norwegian sources count 12 moss species and about 40 lichen species, with no grasses or higher plants.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At least 12 bird species breed on the island, including macaroni and chinstrap penguins.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife paragraph; NPI also gives 12.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Nyrøysa area hosts a colony of about 64,000 Antarctic fur seals, described as the world's second largest, and elephant seals also breed there.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Chinstrap penguin counts at Nyrøysa fell from 2,700 in 1990 to 422 in 1997, probably because fur seals took over penguin territory.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Bouvet is one of few places where no introduced species have been recorded.
facts.source_title: Bouvetøya: nature reserve rules and visitor advice
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife and ecosystem section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Non-native species brought on gear, footwear, soil, food or rodents could outcompete native life, and warming may make conditions more suitable for them.
facts.source_title: Bouvetøya: nature reserve rules and visitor advice
facts.evidence_note: Threats discussion on introduced species.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Growing fur seal numbers appear to be displacing penguins from breeding space at Nyrøysa.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Norwegian authorities call Bouvetøya the world's most remote nature reserve, protected since 1971.
facts.source_title: Bouvetøya: nature reserve rules and visitor advice
facts.evidence_note: Legal protection section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Nyrøysa is a CCAMLR environmental monitoring site, and visits from 1 November to 15 March are limited to approved monitoring.
facts.source_title: Bouvetøya: nature reserve rules and visitor advice
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife and ecosystem section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The macaroni penguin (Eudyptes chrysolophus) is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, based on a 2020 assessment.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status section.
facts.subject: macaroni-penguin

facts.statement: BirdLife South Africa lists the global status as Vulnerable and names Bouvet among the South Atlantic islands where the species breeds.
facts.evidence_note: Global breeding locations paragraph.
facts.subject: macaroni-penguin

facts.statement: Macaroni penguins on Bouvet declined from 5,900 in 1990 to 4,700 in 1997 at Nyrøysa.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife section.
facts.subject: macaroni-penguin

facts.statement: CCAMLR monitoring at Nyrøysa tracks macaroni penguins, reporting a moderate decline since 1989/90.
facts.evidence_note: Population trends section.
facts.subject: macaroni-penguin

facts.statement: The global population is about 6.3 million breeding pairs, and numbers are decreasing.
facts.evidence_note: Population and trend sections.
facts.subject: macaroni-penguin

facts.statement: GBIF's backbone matches Eudyptes chrysolophus as an accepted species with usage key 2481643.
facts.evidence_note: API match result.
facts.subject: macaroni-penguin

facts.statement: The southern giant petrel (Macronectes giganteus), a species covered by the ACAP agreement, once bred in small numbers on Bouvetøya: 20-25 chicks were seen at Nyrøysa in February 1977, and the last breeding record is a single nest seen on 24 January 1981.
facts.source_title: ACAP Breeding Site: Bouvetøya, the World's most remote island, once supported breeding Southern Giant Petrels
facts.publisher: Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP)
facts.evidence_note: Southern Giant Petrel section. The page gives ACAP listing only, not an IUCN Red List category. The nest's contents were not reported.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Expeditions to Bouvetøya in 1989/90, 1996/97, 1998/99, 2000/01, 2001/02, 2007/08 and 2014/15 found no breeding southern giant petrels, although up to 100 birds have been seen scavenging at seal and penguin groups at Nyrøysa since 1981; the page says the reason breeding stopped is unknown.
facts.source_title: ACAP Breeding Site: Bouvetøya, the World's most remote island, once supported breeding Southern Giant Petrels
facts.publisher: Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP)
facts.evidence_note: Southern Giant Petrel section, paragraphs on survey history and cause. The page also says the seal increase came after breeding ended, so seals are unlikely to be the cause; the KBA factsheet instead lists the cessation among effects of fur seal expansion.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia reports that the IUCN moved the Antarctic fur seal (Arctocephalus gazella) from Least Concern to Endangered in April 2026, and lists Bouvet Island as holding the second-largest population, 46,834 animals, with a decreasing trend.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status and population sections. Secondary source; I could not check the IUCN assessment itself. The 46,834 figure is lower than the roughly 64,000 seals in the NPI-based fact BOU-028, so the two sources disagree.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The IMMA factsheet says Bouvet Island hosts the second-largest breeding population of Antarctic fur seals and that Nyrøysa holds about 2.5% of the global breeding population, with pup production stabilizing at about 15,000 pups a year in 1996-2002 (an estimated 66,000 animals at Nyrøysa, the single site monitored on the island).
facts.publisher: IUCN Marine Mammal Protected Areas Task Force
facts.evidence_note: Population information section. Expeditions in 2007, 2014 and 2017 suggest continued stability or a possible slight decline, per the same page. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At Nyrøysa on Bouvetøya, 88 weaned southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) pups were counted in December 1998.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Population numbers section. Count for one site and one season; the IMMA page says consistent counts of this small elephant seal population are lacking.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The KBA factsheet lists the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) as VU (Vulnerable) and records it as frequently sighted from Nyrøysa in 1996-1997 and 1998-1999.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: IUCN categories section. The same page says no recognized globally threatened or endemic animal taxa occur on Bouvetøya, which contradicts its own VU entry, and the category appears to be an older assessment. See the next fact for Wikipedia's 2018 status.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia lists the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) as Least Concern (IUCN 3.1, 2018), with about 135,000 individuals worldwide, and says humpbacks of one stock have been recorded foraging southwest of Africa mainly around Bouvet Island.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status and feeding/range passages; Bouvet mentioned once. This conflicts with the older VU category shown on the KBA factsheet, so both are given.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The KBA factsheet lists the killer whale (Orcinus orca) as LR/cd (Lower Risk, conservation dependent) in its IUCN categories and notes it was previously recorded at Bouvetøya.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: IUCN categories section. LR/cd is an outdated category scheme; the page does not give a current assessment.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Up to 100,000 southern fulmars (Fulmarus glacialoides) are estimated to breed on cliffs on Bouvetøya, according to the KBA factsheet.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Population numbers section gives the 100,000 breeding-bird estimate; The page gives no Red List category; Wikipedia's Southern fulmar page lists the species as Least Concern (IUCN 3.1) and names Bouvet Island as a breeding site. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Chinstrap penguins (Pygoscelis antarctica) at Nyrøysa on Bouvetøya relied almost entirely on Antarctic krill and fell by about 80% over the 1996-97 to 2007-08 study period; the authors call the local chinstrap population probably the most at risk because it is small and has a narrow diet.
facts.source_title: Chinstrap and macaroni penguin diet and demography at Nyrøysa, Bouvetøya
facts.evidence_note: Abstract. Wikipedia lists the chinstrap as Least Concern globally (IUCN 3.1, 2016) and names Bouvet Island as a breeding place; the Cambridge page gives no Red List category.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Instruments on an elephant seal tracked the waters of Bouvetøya's western shelf for 259 days: summer heating built a warm upper layer, a cold layer formed near 100 m as winter advanced, and Upper Circumpolar Deep Water sat near 200 m throughout the year.
facts.source_title: The seasonal evolution of shelf water masses around Bouvetøya, determined from an instrumented southern elephant seal
facts.evidence_note: Abstract (October 2016). The page did not list authors; only one seal's track is described, so it is a single time series for the western shelf.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Bouvetøya and Surrounding Waters Important Marine Mammal Area covers 817,702 km2; lactating Antarctic fur seals from Nyrøysa forage within about 200 km of the island, and waters within a radius of about 400 km serve as foraging grounds for resident and visiting pinnipeds; fur seals feed mainly on krill with some myctophid fish.
facts.publisher: IUCN Marine Mammal Protected Areas Task Force
facts.evidence_note: Area figure at the top and Habitat and oceanography section. The page itself gives two foraging radii, so both are noted. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia says Bouvet Island lies south of the Antarctic Convergence, which by some definitions puts it in the Southern Ocean, and that the sea near the former Thompson Island site is more than 2,400 m deep.
facts.evidence_note: Surrounding ocean passages. The 2021 Cryosphere paper instead places the island within the polar front and calls it sub-Antarctic.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A NASA Earth Observatory astronaut photograph acquired on 13 September 2008 shows abundant sea ice around Bouvet Island.
facts.evidence_note: NASA image caption (sea ice sentence); the caption does not give an ice concentration. Wikipedia separately says the island is surrounded by pack ice in winter. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Sea-ice analysis of the first Bouvet ice core says the island sits on the edge of the median maximum sea ice extent (1981-2010 median, 15% concentration threshold), so in low-ice years it may lie outside the sea ice zone.
facts.source_title: Organic Compounds in a Sub-Antarctic Ice Core: A Potential Suite of Sea Ice Markers
facts.evidence_note: Sea ice extent description in the article; the analysis region was 45-70°S, 50°W to 10°E.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cryosphere ice-core study reports that an automatic weather station at 42 m above sea level on Bouvet Island recorded a maximum temperature of 6.7 °C between 1997 and 2005 (elevation-corrected).
facts.source_title: Physical properties of shallow ice cores from Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands
facts.evidence_note: Temperature section. Wikipedia's 14 °C peak (March 1980) is a different, older record; the two disagree.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 2021 Cryosphere ice-core study gives an elevation-corrected ERA-5 average yearly temperature of -2.9 °C for Bouvet Island (1979-2017), with a maximum monthly temperature of -0.9 °C; this is colder than the -1 °C sea-level mean given by the Norwegian Polar Institute.
facts.source_title: Physical properties of shallow ice cores from Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands
facts.evidence_note: Temperature section. The two values describe different elevations/methods, so they are not a true contradiction. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cryosphere ice-core study measured annual snow accumulation on Bouvet Island at 0.59 m water equivalent, based on annual layer counting of chemical and isotopic species by King et al. (2019).
facts.source_title: Physical properties of shallow ice cores from Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands
facts.evidence_note: Accumulation section of the Bouvet results. The paper does not give a rainfall figure.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Bouvet was the least melt-affected of the sub-Antarctic and Antarctic sites in the Cryosphere ice-core study, which the authors call surprising given its northerly position, with melt layers averaging 0.3 cm thick at about five per metre.
facts.source_title: Physical properties of shallow ice cores from Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands
facts.evidence_note: Melt section; the largest melt layer was 3.95 cm. The Bouvet melt percentage is in an image table I could not read.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Back-trajectory analysis for the Bouvet Island ice core shows that air transport to the site is dominated by westerly winds.
facts.source_title: Organic Compounds in a Sub-Antarctic Ice Core: A Potential Suite of Sea Ice Markers
facts.evidence_note: Five-day back trajectories described in the article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Twelve seabird species are recorded breeding on Bouvetøya; eight have recent confirmed breeding records (Pygoscelis antarctica, Eudyptes chrysolophus, Fulmarus glacialoides, Daption capense, Pachyptila desolata, Oceanites oceanicus, Fregetta tropica and Catharacta antarctica lonnbergi), and the page lists 19 summer-visiting species.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Species section. Adelie penguin, southern giant petrel, snow petrel and Antarctic tern lack recent confirmation. Re-check note: OK: 12 species, eight without recent-record caveat, 19 summer visitors.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: About 93% of Bouvetøya is permanent ice; ice-free ground includes the Nyrøysa platform (about 700 m long and 25-40 m high) and 150-350 m cliffs, with only non-vascular vegetation on coastal cliffs, capes, boulder beaches, nunatak ridges and the summit plateau.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Habitats section. The 93% figure differs from the 89% in Norwegian Polar Institute sources.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The KBA factsheet records at least three endemic ascomycete fungi and three lichens on Bouvetøya, including the endemic genus Bouvetiella, while Wikipedia says six ascomycetes there are endemic.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Species section (non-bird biodiversity). Wikipedia's Bouvet Island page says six ascomycetes (five of them lichens) were recorded at Nyrøysa and that all six are endemic; the counts differ between sources.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Nyrøysa on Bouvetøya hosts 5 moss, 5 lichen, 1 fungus and 20 algae species, and Engelskjøn (1981) sorted the vegetation into 20 communities.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Habitats section. Wikipedia lists five mosses, six ascomycetes and twenty algae for Nyrøysa, a slightly different breakdown.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The KBA factsheet lists fur seal expansion at Nyrøysa as a threat to Bouvetøya's other wildlife, citing competition for breeding territory, injuries in territorial disputes, predation at sea, destruction of Brachythecium moss hummocks, and the end of southern giant petrel breeding.
facts.source_title: Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet: Bouvetøya (Bouvet Island), site 6044
facts.evidence_note: Threats section. A draft management plan for Nyrøysa exists but is not in force; the cause of the petrel decline is disputed by the ACAP page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The ACAP page says Bouvetøya has been a nature reserve with its territorial waters since December 1971, equivalent to IUCN Category Ia, is on Norway's tentative World Heritage list, and is a BirdLife Important Bird Area; it also says Norway has not declared a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, whereas Wikipedia gives an exclusive economic zone of 441,163 km2.
facts.source_title: ACAP Breeding Site: Bouvetøya, the World's most remote island, once supported breeding Southern Giant Petrels
facts.publisher: Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP)
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status section. The EEZ statement conflicts with Wikipedia's Bouvet Island page, so the sources disagree.
facts.subject: island

Last eruption: about 2000 BCE (Wikipedia) vs central crater quiet for several hundred thousand years (SNL)

Station dates: December 2012 (Wikipedia, noted in the fact text) vs January 2014 (SNL)
